methods.label: Count the squares added at each step
methods.explanation:
The figures grow by adding an outer layer. Counting each new layer is easier than counting all the squares in figure \(100\) at once.

In figure \(k-1\), there are \(2k-1\) horizontal rows. To obtain figure \(k\), the displayed pattern adds one square at each end of every existing row, together with one new square above and one below. Thus step \(k\) adds
\[
2(2k-1)+2=4k
\]
squares. These are all the new squares, and squares added at different steps are distinct.

Starting with the single square in figure \(0\), figure \(n\) therefore contains
\[
1+4(1+2+\cdots+n)
\]
squares. To evaluate the sum, write it once in increasing order and once in decreasing order. Each of the \(n\) corresponding pairs sums to \(n+1\), giving
\[
1+2+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}2.
\]
Hence the number of squares in figure \(100\) is
\[
1+4\cdot\frac{100\cdot101}{2}
=1+20200
=\boxed{20201}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: The visual growth rule is justified by counting row endpoints. The consecutive-integer sum is derived by elementary pairing, without requiring formal sequence theory.
